# Abstract

The Burmese macro-region (encompassing 700.767 km² and 8.941 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) supported one of the most durable agrarian civilisations in mainland South-East Asia. Stretching from the rain-shadow expanses of the central Irrawaddy Dry Zone and the forested defiles of the northern river corridors to the fertile deltaic alluvium of the lower Irrawaddy and Sittang rivers, the maritime littoral of Arakan and the karstic valleys of the Shan plateau, early Burmese state formation generated dense settlement networks anchored by monumental masonry and sophisticated hydraulic infrastructure. From early Iron Age walled citadels to the imperial temple metropolis of Pagan and subsequent early modern kingdoms at Inwa, Pegu and Mrauk-U, population dynamics responded directly to seasonal monsoon variability, riverine trade arteries and intensive irrigation works.

Reconstructed across five physiographic and hydrological divisions from 500BC to 1752AD under MANDALA, regional population expanded from 850k inhabitants in 500BC to 1,25M in 0AD and 1,65M in 500AD as early Pyu city-states such as Beikthano, Halin and Sri Ksetra consolidated hydraulic agriculture along alluvial fans. Growth accelerated following the unification of the central plains under the Pagan Empire in the eleventh century AD, reaching 2,2M in 1000AD and attaining an imperial climax of 2,75M inhabitants by 1250AD (yielding an aggregate regional density of 392,43 persons per 100 km²). Following late thirteenth-century hydroclimatic dislocations and Mongol military incursions, regional population contracted to 2,35M in 1300AD before regaining momentum through decentralised post-Pagan polities, expanding to 3,1M in 1500AD, 3,85M in 1600AD and reaching 4,4M inhabitants by 1752AD (yielding a regional density of 627,88 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic mass remained anchored in the Upper Irrawaddy Dry Zone and the Lower Burma Delta. At the 1250AD Pagan climax, the Upper Irrawaddy Dry Zone accommodated 990k people (36% of regional population; 494,93 persons per 100 km²), supported by the Kyaukse and Minbu canal networks and the urban core of Pagan. The Lower Burma Delta and Pegu-Thaton region supported 770k inhabitants (28%; 460,43 persons per 100 km²), anchored by Mon maritime ports and riverine trading settlements. The Shan Plateau accommodated 440k people (16%; 255,66 persons per 100 km²), the Arakan Coastal Kingdom accommodated 302,5k inhabitants (11%; 879,54 persons per 100 km²), and the Northern Irrawaddy and Highland periphery housed 247,5k people (9%; 194,87 persons per 100 km²). During the early modern era, coastal maritime expansion shifted demographic weight towards Lower Burma, where commercial emporia expanded rapidly.

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 170 georeferenced settlement trajectories with remote sensing inventories of ancient hydraulic systems, epigraphic records of monastic land donations and geoarchaeological analyses of masonry monuments. By isolating catalogued urban centres from rural populations, the reconstruction maintains an analytical distinction between civic nucleation and rural cultivators. The trajectory confirms that post-Pagan fragmentation did not constitute a permanent demographic collapse, but rather a geographic redistribution of administrative weight towards fertile deltaic channels and maritime trade routes.

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology and Environmental Gradients

The geographic architecture of Burma is defined by north-to-south trending river corridors bounded by rugged mountain cordilleras [@Miksic2001Early; @Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Goodrich1971History]. The Irrawaddy River, originating in the eastern Himalayan foothills of Kachin, forms the central spine of the region, flowing more than two thousand kilometres to empty into the Andaman Sea through an expansive nine-armed delta. Parallel to the lower Irrawaddy lies the Sittang River, which drains the eastern Pegu Yoma into the Gulf of Martaban, while the Salween River cuts through deep karstic gorges across the Shan Plateau.

The most defining climatic feature of central Burma is the Dry Zone, an arid rain-shadow basin enclosed between the Arakan Yoma to the west and the Shan Plateau to the east [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Macrae2022Ancient]. While coastal Arakan and the lower delta receive annual south-west monsoon rainfall exceeding 2.500 mm, the Dry Zone receives less than 800 mm annually. Successful sedentary agriculture in this core basin depended entirely on seasonal tributary streams, perennial river diversion and hydraulic storage systems [@Macrae2022Ancient]. The alluvial fans formed by rivers descending from the eastern plateau into the Irrawaddy, notably the Samon, Panlaung and Zawgyi rivers in Kyaukse and the Salin and Mon rivers in Minbu, provided fertile silts and perennial waters that sustained intensive double-cropped paddy rice [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Gutman2023Archaeolog].

West of the Irrawaddy basin, the Arakan coastal strip forms a narrow littoral zone bounded by steep mountain ridges and intersected by estuarine channels and tidal creeks [@Miksic2001Early; @Griffiths2015Three; @Charney1998Rise]. Nourished by heavy monsoon precipitation, fertile alluvial plains along the Kaladan and Lemro rivers supported early rice farming and sheltered maritime anchorages. To the east, the Shan Plateau rises abruptly to elevations between 1.000 and 2.000 metres, presenting karstic limestone plateaux dissected by upland river basins where sawbwa principalities developed around fertile alluvial pockets.

The northern perimeter comprises rugged highland ranges spanning the Chin Hills, the Naga Hills and the upper Irrawaddy headwaters around Bhamo [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Goodrich1971History]. These upland valleys served as critical transit zones for overland caravan trade between south-western China (Yunnan) and the central plains of Burma, channelling jade, amber, silk and metal ores into regional markets.

## Prehistoric Foundations and the Pyu City-States

The transition from late Neolithic foraging to sedentary farming was concentrated along the alluvial fans of the central Dry Zone [@Miksic2001Early; @Khaing2022Neolithic; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. Excavations across the Samon Valley and central basin document Bronze Age and Iron Age cemetery horizons characterised by bronze lance points, socketed axes, carnelian beads and bronze wire ornaments [@Miksic2001Early; @San2018Physical; @Stargardt2016Iron]. By the middle of the first millennium BC, nucleated agricultural communities coalesced into fortified urban settlements known collectively as the Pyu city-states [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Nyunt2015Ancient].

The Pyu cities represented the earliest large-scale urban culture in mainland South-East Asia [@Miksic2001Early; @Stargardt2016Iron; @Nyunt2015Ancient]. Major centres developed distinctive circular or oval perimeter walls constructed from massive kiln-fired bricks:
1. Beikthano, situated in the Yin Valley near Taungdwingyi, emerged as an early ceremonial and administrative centre enclosed by a brick wall measuring 3 km by 1 km, featuring monumental brick gateways and compartmentalised storage structures dating from the second century BC to the fifth century AD [@Stargardt2016Iron; @San2018Physical].
2. Halin, positioned in the Mu River valley of Upper Burma, encompassed a rectangular walled perimeter of 5 km² equipped with defensive curved gates, brick stupas and extensive cremation burial urn fields inscribed with early Pyu script [@Miksic2001Early; @Frasch2024Urns; @Hudson2024Funerary].
3. Sri Ksetra, located near modern Pyay along the lower reach of the central Dry Zone, grew into the largest Pyu metropolis, enclosed by a massive circular brick rampart enclosing 14 km² [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Stargardt2015Urban; @Indasiha2026History].
4. Maingmaw, located in the Kyaukse plain near the Panlaung River, functioned as a circular fortified hub coordinating early irrigation channels in the eastern piedmont [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Miksic2001Early].

Hydraulic engineering was integral to Pyu urban planning [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Nyunt2015Ancient; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. Rather than building large canal networks along the main stem of the Irrawaddy, Pyu engineers trapped seasonal torrents debouching from highland ridges using earthen bunds, curved diversion weirs and urban moat circuits. These systems channelled floodwaters into interior storage tanks and peripheral fields, insulating urban populations against seasonal droughts [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. Pyu society was characterised by Theravada and Mahayana Buddhist religious institutions, evidenced by gold-leaf Pali manuscripts, votive tablets and monumental sandstone stelae depicting warrior-rulers and royal genealogies [@Indasiha2026History; @Hudson2024Funerary; @Frasch2024Urns].

## The Pagan Empire and Agrarian Climax

During the ninth and tenth centuries AD, political dominance shifted north to Pagan (Bagan), strategically sited on the eastern bank of the Irrawaddy River in the heart of the Dry Zone [@Miksic2001Early; @Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Jaremba2022History]. Under King Anawrahta (reigned 1044AD to 1077AD) and his successors Kyansittha and Alaungsithu, Pagan unified the disparate riverine and coastal polities into the first centralised Burmese empire [@Goodrich1971History; @FraserLu2016Lacquered; @Indasiha2026History_2].

The economic foundation of Pagan rested upon the systematic expansion of state-managed irrigation networks in Kyaukse (the Eleven Ledwin districts) and Minbu (the Six Ledwin districts) [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Merit; @Iannone2020Entangleme]. Royal administrators constructed stone weirs, masonry sluice gates and contoured canals that diverted mountain runoff across tens of thousands of hectares of fertile alluvium [@Macrae2022Ancient]. The grain surplus generated by these hydraulic systems supported an unprecedented concentration of artisans, religious specialists and court officials at the capital [@Iannone2020Merit; @Iannone2020Entangleme].

Between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries AD, the kings, queens and high-ranking courtiers of Pagan dedicated massive wealth to Buddhist religious foundations [@Iannone2020Merit; @Indasiha2026History_2; @Bailey1971Burma]. Across a 40 km² urban plain, more than 3.000 monumental temples, stupas and monastic complexes were erected from kiln-fired brick and lime plaster [@San2018Physical; @Hudson2008Restoratio; @Bianchini2020Seismic]. Structures such as the Ananda, Thatbyinnyu, Gawdawpalin and Dhammayangyi temples incorporated advanced vaulted masonry arches, terracotta relief plaques depicting Jataka tales and intricate mural paintings reflecting cosmopolitan Buddhist iconographies [@Hudson2008Restoratio; @Yeom2016Formal; @Bailey1971Burma]. Epigraphic records carved on stone stelae document the transfer of irrigated land (*kwin*), hereditary service personnel (*kywan*) and storage granaries to monastic institutions, establishing a durable socio-economic infrastructure that supported dense rural settlement [@John1914Inscriptions; @Hertz1929Selections; @Iannone2020Merit].

Astrological and cosmological planning governed the spatial orientation of royal palaces, city walls and temple complexes [@Indasiha2026History_2; @Yeom2016Formal; @Bailey1971Burma]. City layouts mirrored Buddhist cosmological geography, with central palace enclosures symbolising Mount Meru, surrounded by moat networks that represented cosmic oceans, aligning dynastic legitimacy with sacred space [@Yeom2016Formal; @Indasiha2026History_2].

## Thirteenth-Century Dislocation and Post-Pagan Restructuring

The demographic climax of the Pagan Empire was interrupted in the late thirteenth century AD by an intersection of environmental stress, fiscal strain and foreign invasion [@Iannone2020Entangleme; @Iannone2020Merit; @Macrae2022Ancient]. Decades of continuous tax-exempt land donations to Buddhist monasteries progressively eroded the royal fiscal base, reducing the crown's capacity to maintain regional hydraulic infrastructure [@Iannone2020Merit; @Iannone2020Entangleme].

Concurrently, high-resolution palaeoclimatic records derived from tree-ring chronologies and speleothem profiles reveal that mainland South-East Asia experienced severe multi-year monsoon failures during the mid-to-late thirteenth century AD, alternating with catastrophic flash flooding [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Entangleme]. These climatic anomalies compromised weir operations across Kyaukse and Minbu, triggering localised grain shortages. When Mongol armies launched punitive expeditions into northern Burma between 1277AD and 1287AD, sacking Pagan and dismantling the central royal court, the imperial administrative structure collapsed [@Jaremba2022History; @Gutman2023Archaeolog].

Regional population receded from 2,75M in 1250AD to 2,35M in 1300AD. However, this disruption did not lead to permanent de-population. Instead, demographic mass reconstituted around new regional centres:
1. In Upper Burma, Burmese and Shan-Burman rulers established fortified river capitals at Pinya, Sagaing and Inwa (Ava), commanding the confluence of the Irrawaddy and Myitnge rivers [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Goodrich1971History; @Jaremba2022History].
2. In Lower Burma, the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy established its capital at Pegu (Bago), capitalising on growing Indian Ocean maritime commerce and expanding deltaic rice cultivation [@AungThwin2002Lower; @McCormick2011Position].
3. In Arakan, the Mrauk-U Kingdom emerged as a formidable coastal power along the Kaladan estuary, combining hill fortifications with a powerful naval fleet and participating in Bay of Bengal trading circuits [@Charney1998Rise; @Charney1998Crisis; @dHubert2015Lord].
4. Across the eastern uplands, Shan sawbwas consolidated autonomous valley fiefdoms linked to trans-plateau caravan routes connecting Upper Burma with Yunnan and the Tai principalities [@Tongkamwan1961Inscription; @Goodrich1971History].

During the sixteenth century AD, the Taungoo Dynasty unified these fragmented regions, establishing a powerful military state under King Bayinnaung (reigned 1550AD to 1581AD) that commanded maritime trade revenues from Pegu and agricultural revenues from Upper Burma [@AungThwin2002Lower; @Goodrich1971History]. This political consolidation spurred steady demographic recovery, reaching 3,85M in 1600AD and 4,4M by 1752AD prior to the rise of the Konbaung Dynasty.

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 700.767 km² of diverse terrain, MANDALA partitions the Burmese macro-region into 8.941 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated using continuous environmental suitability surfaces:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to the Irrawaddy, Chindwin, Sittang and Kaladan river corridors, with exponential density attenuation beyond 12 km in non-irrigated upland tracts [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Macrae2022Ancient].
- Alluvial soil masking: high weighting for active floodplains, river terraces and deltaic fans capable of supporting wet-rice agriculture.
- Topographic slope penalties: severe penalisation of steep, inaccessible terrain in the Arakan Yoma, Chin Hills and eastern Shan scarps, favouring valley floors, piedmont plains and coastal flats.
- Monsoon precipitation and drought risk: integrating seasonal rainfall indices to capture the contrasting agrarian constraints between the semi-arid Dry Zone and the hyper-humid delta and Arakan littoral [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Gutman2023Archaeolog].

Terrain elevation data from digital elevation models were combined with soil drainage profiles to differentiate between inundated backswamps, well-drained levee crests and rocky pediments. This environmental stratification ensures that dasymetric allocations accurately reflect local carrying capacities.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To prevent artificial clustering and avoid double-counting between urban centres and agricultural cultivators, 170 catalogued settlements are georeferenced to WGS84 coordinates. Each settlement possesses an active demographic trajectory reflecting historical foundations, expansions and abandonments.

At each benchmark year, the active population of all catalogued settlements within a sub-region is aggregated and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope. The remaining population represents the rural agricultural base, which is dasymetrically distributed across non-settled pixels in accordance with environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary smoothing filter feathers transitions across sub-regional borders, ensuring realistic continuous density gradients without artificial boundary cliffs.

This two-tier procedure separates concentrated civic populations from dispersed farming hamlets, enabling direct spatial comparison between nucleated political capitals and surrounding agrarian hinterlands.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Demographic reconstructions across pre-colonial Burma carry inherent uncertainty arising from taphonomic preservation, variable settlement sizes and epigraphic recording gaps [@Miksic2001Early; @Hudson2014Myanmar]. To represent these bounds analytically, each benchmark estimate includes symmetric uncertainty envelopes calibrated to historical source confidence:
- Early benchmarks (500BC to 500AD): +/- 25% uncertainty, reflecting reliance on archaeological mound dimensions, brick wall circuits and cemetery extents [@Stargardt2016Iron; @San2018Physical; @Frasch2024Urns].
- Classical benchmarks (1000AD to 1300AD): +/- 20% uncertainty, calibrated against stone epigraphy, temple clusters and canal capacities [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Entangleme; @Hertz1929Selections].
- Early modern benchmarks (1500AD to 1752AD): +/- 15% uncertainty, constrained by revenue inquests (*sittans*), military muster rolls and European travel accounts [@Charney1998Rise; @AungThwin2002Lower; @Goodrich1971History].

# Testing and Validation

## Archaeological Settlement Surveys and Brick Architecture

The catalogued settlement trajectories were verified through comparison with published archaeological excavations and regional monument surveys [@Miksic2001Early; @San2018Physical; @Hudson2008Restoratio; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. In Pyu and Pagan urban centres, brick typology provides an independent chronometric benchmark [@San2018Physical]. Pyu bricks from Beikthano and Sri Ksetra are exceptionally large (averaging 45 by 22 by 8 cm) and frequently carry incised finger-stroke motifs applied before firing, whereas Pagan bricks exhibit smaller, standardised modular dimensions (averaging 35 by 18 by 5 cm) suited to load-bearing vaulted arches [@San2018Physical; @Stargardt2016Iron; @Gutman2023Archaeolog].

Petrographic and chemical characterisations of ancient brick fabrics by San and colleagues demonstrate that Pagan monuments utilised local silty clays tempered with sand and rice husks, fired in wood-burning updraft kilns along river terraces [@San2018Physical]. The immense volume of brick masonry surviving across the Pagan plain (exceeding hundreds of thousands of cubic metres) corroborates the large artisan populations recorded in contemporary inscriptions and supports civic population estimates of over 100k inhabitants at the capital's peak [@San2018Physical; @Miksic2001Early].

Digital architectural recording and photogrammetric modelling by Bianchini and colleagues demonstrate that structural stability in masonry monuments relied on advanced lime mortars and brick interlocking systems, providing physical evidence for specialised state construction guilds and large-scale labour mobilisations [@Bianchini2020Seismic; @Hudson2008Restoratio].

## Remote Sensing and Hydraulic Network Analysis

Remote sensing analysis using synthetic aperture radar and multitemporal multispectral satellite imagery has revealed extensive buried canals, palaeochannels and earthen reservoirs across the Dry Zone [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Hudson2014Myanmar]. At Sri Ksetra, satellite mapping confirmed that the city's circular ramparts were integrated into an elaborate regional water diversion network that guided storm runoff from the southern hills through walled sluices into urban moats and agricultural tanks [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Stargardt2015Urban; @Liljeblad2020World].

In Kyaukse, aerial surveys identified over 300 kilometres of ancient stone-lined canals branching from the Panlaung and Zawgyi rivers, verifying the traditional accounts of the Eleven Ledwin irrigation canals recorded in royal chronicles [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Goodrich1971History]. The spatial alignment between mapped canal networks and catalogued settlement locations confirms that rural demographic density was tightly tethered to engineered water infrastructure [@Macrae2022Ancient].

Archaeological field investigations and hydrological surveys by Macrae and colleagues confirm that ancient water diversion structures and earthen bunds remained functional across centuries of rural cultivation, establishing the long-term continuity of hydraulic field organisation [@Macrae2022Ancient].

## Epigraphic Calibration and Agrarian Multi-Cropping

Inscriptions inscribed on polished stone slabs provide contemporaneous socio-demographic data for the Pagan and Inwa periods [@John1914Inscriptions; @Hertz1929Selections; @Bailey1971Burma]. Over 1.500 surviving Old Burmese, Mon and Sanskrit inscriptions record the precise boundaries of agricultural estates, the number of dedicated serfs (*kywan*), storage granaries and seasonal grain yields [@Hertz1929Selections; @John1914Inscriptions; @Iannone2020Merit].

These inscriptions confirm that irrigated lands in Kyaukse and Minbu yielded two paddy crops annually, supplemented by dry-season sesame, pulses and cotton [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Merit; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. This double-cropping agricultural regime achieved caloric yields capable of sustaining population densities exceeding 400 persons per square kilometre in irrigated core tracts, providing direct calibration for the sub-regional population envelopes adopted in MANDALA [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Merit].

Epigraphic studies by Hertz, Pe Maung Tin and Luce on Old Burmese donor inscriptions document that monastic foundations directly supervised communal irrigation maintenance, ensuring that agricultural infrastructure remained functional across generational successions [@Hertz1929Selections; @Iannone2020Merit].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA settlement gazetteer was assembled through a four-stage asymptotic ingestion process:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national archaeological registers and heritage inventories, identifying 105 primary historical settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of site catalogues from archaeological monographs, architectural registers and excavation reports, adding 46 regional centres and ports.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 19 early Iron Age and upland sawbwa settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym deduplication sweeps across all five sub-regions, confirming asymptotic saturation with zero newly identified eligible sites (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 209 candidate localities were evaluated: 170 were accepted as catalogued settlements and 39 were excluded (primarily duplicate pagoda monuments or modern suburbs lying within a 2,2 km deduplication radius).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The long-term demographic trajectory of the Burmese macro-region across 2.250 years exhibits a multi-phased path characterised by early urban expansion, imperial consolidation, late thirteenth-century disruption and early modern re-expansion (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Historical Demographic Epochs

### Proto-Urban Gestation and Pyu City-States (500BC to 800AD)

During the first millennium BC and the early first millennium AD, demographic growth was concentrated in the alluvial fans of the central Dry Zone [@Miksic2001Early; @Stargardt2016Iron; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. Regional population expanded from 850k in 500BC to 1,25M in 0AD and 1,65M by 500AD. The period witnessed the rise of walled Pyu city-states: Beikthano emerged as an early ceremonial centre (13,71k in 0AD), Halin dominated the northern Mu valley (15,33k in 500AD), and Sri Ksetra grew into a metropolis along the southern Irrawaddy reach (34,07k in 500AD) [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Stargardt2015Urban; @Nyunt2015Ancient]. Along the coast, early Mon settlements formed around Thaton (12,21k in 500AD), while Dhanyawadi developed as an independent capital in Arakan (14,53k in 500AD) [@AungThwin2002Lower; @Griffiths2015Three].

Urban layout and defensive architecture were reinforced by massive earth-core brick ramparts and gated moats [@Stargardt2016Iron; @Gutman2023Archaeolog]. Royal funerary urns, stone stelae and calendar inscriptions document dynastic lineages presiding over specialised artisan and agricultural populations [@Frasch2024Urns; @Hudson2024Funerary; @Indasiha2026History].

### Classical Imperial Unification at Pagan (800AD to 1250AD)

Between 800AD and 1250AD, the unification of Upper and Lower Burma under the Pagan dynasty triggered substantial population expansion [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Jaremba2022History; @Goodrich1971History]. Regional numbers climbed from 1,65M in 500AD to 2,2M in 1000AD, reaching an imperial apex of 2,75M inhabitants by 1250AD. Pagan expanded into a sprawling imperial capital concentrating 102,16k inhabitants in 1000AD and 77,97k in 1250AD [@Miksic2001Early; @San2018Physical; @Hudson2008Restoratio]. The Upper Irrawaddy Dry Zone supported 990k people by 1250AD, sustained by the Kyaukse and Minbu irrigation canal complexes [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Merit]. Monastic endowments registered thousands of rural serfs, creating an integrated agricultural surplus economy [@Hertz1929Selections; @Iannone2020Merit; @Indasiha2026History_2].

Excavations of industrial ceramic sites along the Shwe Creek in Pagan by Lin and Phyu Thant demonstrate extensive utilitarian earthenware production, corroborating high domestic consumption demand in the civic core [@Lin2025Preliminary]. Pagoda typologies and vaulted brick architecture classified by Yeom, Cheon and Kim reflect standardised royal building programmes across consecutive reigns [@Yeom2016Formal; @Hudson2008Restoratio].

### Thirteenth-Century Dislocation and Multi-Centric Polities (1250AD to 1500AD)

Between 1250AD and 1300AD, consecutive monsoon failures, fiscal exhaustion and Mongol military campaigns disrupted the Pagan administrative core [@Macrae2022Ancient; @Iannone2020Entangleme; @Jaremba2022History]. Total population dropped by 14,5% from 2,75M in 1250AD to 2,35M in 1300AD. Pagan itself declined to 66k inhabitants by 1300AD. As imperial centralisation dissolved, demographic recovery occurred through multi-centric polities. In Upper Burma, Inwa (Ava) was founded in 1364AD and grew to 80,15k inhabitants by 1500AD [@Gutman2023Archaeolog; @Goodrich1971History]. In Lower Burma, the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy transformed Pegu into a thriving commercial capital (129,58k in 1500AD), while Mrauk-U concentrated 95,43k inhabitants in Arakan [@AungThwin2002Lower; @Charney1998Rise; @dHubert2015Lord]. By 1500AD, regional population rebounded to 3,1M inhabitants.

Chronicles such as the Glass Palace Chronicle and royal epigraphic records document diplomatic missions and monastic exchanges among these rival regional courts, reflecting a durable multipolar political equilibrium [@FraserLu2016Lacquered; @McCormick2011Position].

### Early Modern Re-Integration and Commercial Expansion (1500AD to 1752AD)

The sixteenth through eighteenth centuries AD witnessed the re-unification of Burma under the Taungoo Dynasty and the integration of the kingdom into maritime Indian Ocean trade [@Goodrich1971History; @AungThwin2002Lower]. Regional population expanded from 3,1M in 1500AD to 3,85M in 1600AD, attaining 4,4M inhabitants by 1752AD. Pegu peaked at 136,67k inhabitants around 1600AD as the imperial capital of King Bayinnaung, while Toungoo housed 37,21k people [@AungThwin2002Lower; @Goodrich1971History]. Mrauk-U reached 117,57k inhabitants in 1600AD, commanding coastal maritime commerce in the Bay of Bengal before facing internal succession crises and administrative restructuring in the seventeenth century [@Charney1998Rise; @Charney1998Crisis; @dHubert2015Lord]. In the delta, Yangon (Dagon) expanded from a regional shrine centre into an expansive commercial port, reaching 393,79k inhabitants by 1752AD. In Upper Burma, Inwa maintained 82,87k residents in 1600AD and 57,06k in 1752AD, while neighbouring Mandalay plain settlements expanded to 70,04k inhabitants.

The urban settlement hierarchy conformed to four structural tiers:
1. Imperial Metropolises (> 100k inhabitants): Yangon (393,79k peak in 1752AD), Pegu (136,67k in 1600AD), Mrauk-U (117,57k in 1600AD) and Pagan (102,16k in 1000AD). These cities functioned as multi-functional imperial capitals, coordinating religious administration, royal armies and maritime or riverine trade.
2. Major Regional Capitals (30k to 100k inhabitants): Inwa (82,87k in 1600AD), Mandalay plain (70,04k in 1752AD), Hlaingthaya (39,88k in 1752AD), Toungoo (37,21k in 1600AD) and Sri Ksetra (34,07k in 500AD). These centres commanded strategic river confluences and tributary grain districts.
3. Secondary Fortified Towns (10k to 30k inhabitants): Chin State hillfort clusters (21,12k in 1752AD), Kalay (20,21k in 1752AD), Kayah State upland centres (16,81k in 1752AD), Halin (15,33k in 500AD), Dhanyawadi (14,53k in 500AD), Insein (14,36k in 1752AD), Amarapura (13,78k in 1752AD), Pathein (13,75k in 1752AD), Beikthano (13,71k in 0AD), Thaton (12,21k in 500AD), Maingmaw (11,23k in 500AD), Monywa (10,55k in 1752AD), Kyaukpyu (10,44k in 1752AD), Meiktila (10,29k in 1752AD) and Myeik (10,05k in 1752AD).
4. Tertiary Agrarian and Caravan Towns (< 10k inhabitants): Keng Tung (9,95k in 1752AD), Mu-se (9,57k in 1752AD), Dawei (8,78k in 1752AD), Myingyan (8,22k in 1752AD), Pyay (7,84k in 1752AD), Ann (6,94k in 1752AD), Moeng Yang (6,79k in 1752AD) and dozens of riverine market villages.

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis across early Burma is subject to several methodological and taphonomic constraints:
1. Preservation of organic domestic architecture: while monumental temples, stupas and palace platforms were constructed from kiln-fired brick and dressed stone, domestic dwellings across all periods were built from timber, bamboo and thatch [@San2018Physical; @Miksic2001Early; @Hudson2014Myanmar]. Residential quarters leave minimal surface topography, requiring reliance on wall enclosures, pottery scatters and roof-tile scatters to estimate habitation areas.
2. Alluvial burial and channel migration: dynamic seasonal sedimentation along the lower Irrawaddy and Sittang rivers has buried early Mon and Pyu occupational layers beneath metres of silt [@Miksic2001Early; @Stargardt2015Urban]. Conversely, lateral river meandering has undercut and eroded riverfront sections of historical walled cities, including sectors of Inwa and Pagan.
3. Epigraphic geographic concentration: stone inscriptions are overwhelmingly concentrated in religious foundations of the central Dry Zone, particularly Pagan and Inwa [@Hertz1929Selections; @John1914Inscriptions; @Indasiha2026History_2]. Peripheral upland valleys in Shan and Kachin territories left fewer durable textual records, necessitating greater reliance on trade registers, colonial gazetteers and topological projections [@Goodrich1971History; @Tongkamwan1961Inscription].
4. Monastic serfdom accounting: stone stelae register serfs (*kywan*) and dedicated lands transferred to monasteries, but rural freeholder cultivators (*athi*) are less consistently enumerated, introducing potential undercounting in non-donated royal domains [@Hertz1929Selections; @Iannone2020Merit].

# Conclusion

The demographic history of Burma from 500BC to 1752AD reveals a sustained trajectory of agrarian expansion and institutional development. From early Pyu city-states exploiting seasonal stream diversions in the Dry Zone, regional society expanded into an integrated imperial realm under Pagan, supported by the Kyaukse and Minbu canal complexes and an enduring culture of monumental brick construction.

The thirteenth-century crisis demonstrated the sensitivity of central states to hydroclimatic fluctuations and fiscal depletion. Yet the dissolution of Pagan did not terminate urban life; rather, demographic mass decentralised into vigorous regional kingdoms at Inwa, Pegu and Mrauk-U, setting the stage for early modern commercial resurgence under the Taungoo Dynasty. By integrating georeferenced settlement trajectories with environmental suitability surfaces, MANDALA captures both the resilience of rural cultivators and the strategic reorientation of urban networks across two millennia of Burmese history.
